item.title: What to sort out before the money lands
item.description:
Two philanthropic advisers on how sudden wealth affects you, and the three things to set up now.

Right now, an unusually large number of people in tech are on the edge of an extreme wealth event. Through a tender offer, IPO, acquisition, or vesting equity, they will go from a salary to tens or hundreds of millions of dollars almost overnight. This post is for them.

We are Jack Lewars of Ultra Philanthropy and Chloe Cockburn of Just Impact Advisors, two philanthropic advisors with 18 years of combined experience. Jack focuses mainly on global health; Chloe focuses on U.S. criminal justice reform. We have watched many people go through this transition, and we've seen people make avoidable mistakes. Our goal is to help you feel less overwhelmed and more prepared before the money arrives.

As we each run a philanthropic fund, we could benefit if you follow some of this advice. Weigh it accordingly.

If you only have a minute, make a plan now to do these three things:

  1. Pick a small group of trusted friends and advisors, and ask them today to help keep you on track.
  2. Talk to a tax advisor before any liquidity event. Some of the biggest decisions, like how and when to give shares, can't be undone after a sale.
  3. Write down two numbers: how much you'll give in your first year (we suggest at least 1% of your wealth), and how much of your time you want to spend on giving.

How will sudden wealth affect me?

You don't need to become "the type of person who has extreme wealth," whatever that image means to you. You are the same person you were six months ago. However, the money will change how the world relates to you.

You will no longer get honest feedback. Almost everyone around you will have a strong incentive to keep you happy and stay in your good graces. Very few people will tell you an idea is bad, and almost no one will point out a mistake. Without feedback, it gets harder to stay considerate, keep growing, make good decisions, and, above all, course-correct from bad ones.

It can get lonely. Wealth doesn't make you less human. You can still feel sadness, doubt, and fear. But people are rarely sympathetic to a rich person who is struggling, especially when the wealth itself is the cause. That makes it hard to talk openly, which can lead to isolation.

You may struggle to find purpose. If you've spent years driving toward professional success and financial independence, "making it" can leave a surprising vacuum. What now?

You'll face a flood of requests and decisions. You'll suddenly be able to solve many problems, for people you love and for the wider world. That can be exhilarating, and also overwhelming: where do you start, and where do you stop? Everyone in your life, and many strangers, will know you could help them. Meanwhile, the setup phase brings an enormous number of decisions.

Each of these challenges has a practical response, and most of them work best if you put them in place early.

What should I do before the money arrives?

Choose your inner circle now

The most important thing you can do is surround yourself with people who respect your humanity, whom you can be open with, and, most of all, who will challenge bad ideas. Choose them in advance. Look for:

  • people who don't venerate wealth for its own sake;
  • people who knew and understood you before you were rich;
  • people with the character and skill to give you honest feedback; and
  • advisors who have worked with others through sudden wealth.

Make feedback routine

Unless you proactively ask for feedback, don't expect anyone to give you any, ever. And unless you encourage critical feedback specifically, and show people that it's safe and even rewarded for them to share it with you, any feedback you get will be extremely gentle.

You will need to create a structure and the right incentives to receive feedback. This can be as simple as having a standing agenda item for feedback from an advisor or friend you meet regularly, so that it is easy for them to raise things, and committing to being open and thoughtful in response. You can also include giving feedback explicitly in the remit or performance targets of anyone you employ.

Tell your wealth managers what you actually want

You'll need wealth managers to organize your assets and handle taxes. Remember that their job is to protect and grow your money, and they are usually paid a percentage of the assets they manage. Absent specific instructions, they will work to keep money in your name.

If growing your wealth isn't your goal, find managers who will support other goals, and give them explicit direction. For example: up to $X for your own living costs, up to $Y for the people in your life, and the remaining $Z to give away. Make those numbers explicit. 

Get tax advice before any liquidity event

In the US and UK, giving appreciated shares to charity, including a donor-advised fund, generally lets you avoid capital gains tax on them and deduct their full market value. That often works best before a sale or IPO is locked in, because once a sale is effectively certain, some of the benefit may be lost. Where you live, how you set up trusts, and how much you give in which tax year can also make a big difference. Rules differ between jurisdictions, so talk to a tax advisor with charitable-planning experience before the money lands.

Set a system for personal requests

We often hear newly wealthy people ask: how do I handle friends and family asking me for money? We suggest that you create a simple policy, so that every ask doesn't become an agonizing judgment call. You can change it later. Two examples:

  • Say yes to any request up to $5,000 without deliberating, capped at $100,000 per year.
  • Proactively give a set amount to the people closest to you, and make clear there won't be further gifts for at least a year.

Either approach gives you breathing room. It also spares people close to you from feeling they need to choose between your friendship and asking for money they genuinely need.

Tighten your security and privacy

Once word of your wealth spreads, you may be the target of scams, phishing aimed at your accounts, unsolicited pitches, and occasionally physical risks. There are security consultants who can help you manage this, but a few tips are: lock down your accounts with hardware security keys; think twice before sharing your finances or whereabouts publicly. If you'd rather give quietly, some vehicles, like donor-advised funds, allow you to give anonymously.

How should I approach philanthropy after a liquidity event?

Giving can answer several of the challenges above at once. It offers a new source of purpose. Distributing money can relieve the burden on you. It's a rational response to having enormous abundance while seeing deprivation around you. And it can keep your relationships more normal: if people know you've committed most of your wealth to charity, especially through an irrevocable vehicle like a donor-advised fund, fewer of them will see you as a solution to their problems.

Get money moving in year one

The most common pattern we see is a donor who makes a plan and then doesn't follow through, because work and the other demands of the transition take up so much time and energy. Leaving philanthropic money unspent becomes a burden for you and a real loss for the causes it could have helped.

Whatever your long-term plans, commit to getting a set amount out of the door in your first year. We suggest at least 1% of your wealth as a baseline, given to organizations rather than parked indefinitely in a donor-advised fund. You can certainly go higher than 1%: this number is meant to be small (compared to your total giving capacity), yet meaningful in dollars, to get you past the initial hesitation around giving. The easiest way to do this is to hand an initial amount to people you trust, so your money starts helping right away while you figure out the structure that suits you.

Delegate more than feels natural

Going from excellent engineer or founder to skillful philanthropist is a long journey, and it may not be your comparative advantage. Most of the world's most impactful philanthropists delegate heavily, through expert-led funds or by hiring staff. You don't have to drop everything and go all-in with your time.

Philanthropy is unusual in that experts are often expected to defer to the client, even if they believe the client is wrong. Losing a client's goodwill is too big a risk, so advisors tend to tell clients what they want to hear to keep the work going. That's a problem, because, on most grant decisions, a good fund manager or field expert knows more about the grantee and the field than the donor does. Second, money creates change mainly when it follows a coherent strategy. On this point, while we encourage delegation, be mindful that generalist consulting firms often tap into expert knowledge for recommendations, but lack the knowledge in the cause area to combine those grants into an impactful portfolio. 

One type of delegation involves giving to expert-led philanthropic funds, which have several benefits. You can access expertise without having to hire someone; you can make a one-time contribution rather than having to stick with something for years, and you spread the risk with other donors. Giving through funds also ensures that if you change direction in a few years, you won’t have to massively disappoint grantees when you stop giving, which is a hazard of giving directly to organizations. 

Separate your money from your time

Many donors want to be "more than a check." We suggest treating these as two separate questions. Your skills and interests are not automatically  useful to the causes that can most benefit from your funding, and the two do not have to come as a package. 

Think carefully before making giving your whole identity

Making philanthropy your entire purpose has real downsides. It can lead you to micromanage your team. It can slow your giving, because who are you once the money is gone? And it can fill your life with meetings and conferences full of people thinking about your money, which is draining.

We suggest deciding early how much time you want to spend on giving; that choice should shape your whole process. Be honest about which decisions you're equipped to make. Donors are rarely the best final decision-makers on strategy, hiring, theory of change, or evaluation, though they can contribute to all of them.

Finally, if you hire someone to lead your giving, make sure their style matches yours. We often see new donors from tech hire a foundation director steeped in conventional philanthropy, then discover a mismatch in pace, boldness, and analytical rigor. Pick someone aligned with your risk tolerance and ambition.

Why start planning now?

Coming into extreme wealth can feel daunting and, when you're working flat out, it's tempting to put off thinking about it. 

However, some decisions, like tax timing, can't be undone, and others are easier to make beforehand than retroactively. 

Start with the three steps at the top of this post: choose your people, talk to a tax advisor, and write down your first-year giving and time commitments. That will give you a solid foundation for the opportunities and challenges to come.

Jack Lewars is the founder of Ultra Philanthropy, an independent advisory that helps major donors give for maximum impact, and is the fund manager of its Mid-Stage Global Health Fund. He advises donors giving up to nine figures a year, and is Chair of Trustees at High Impact Athletes. Talk to him about your giving.

Chloe Cockburn is the founder of Just Impact Advisors, an independent advisory, and is the fund manager of the Just Impact Fund, launched with an initial major contribution from Open Philanthropy (now Coefficient Giving), whose focus is on reducing incarceration in the United States. In addition to running the fund and advising donors on this cause area, she provides general strategy consulting and support to donors getting oriented. You can read her Substack here and contact her here. 

We used Claude to suggest improvements and flag gaps, as well as for proofreading. All opinions, primary drafting, and final edits are ours.

item.title: VPD's Evaluation Adversary Finds Systematic Defects in the Released Decomposition
item.description:
TL;DR: adVersarial Parameter Decomposition (VPD) decomposes model weights into simple components and assigns labels that specify whether a component is needed for a given input. A core aspiration of VPD is robust mechanistic faithfulness - the property that switching off any set of unneeded components for a given input leaves the model's output approximately unchanged. The authors use an evaluation adversary to measure the degree of robustness, and report that the decomposition is not at all robust to very long adversarial searches. The authors list this as a limitation, but also argue that complete robustness is not necessarily the goal. Their discussion implies two conditions under which a lack of robustness at large step counts may not matter in practice: 1) the adversary could be finding defects in the decomposition that are tuned to particular inputs, rather than systematically carrying over to other inputs, or 2) the masks a practitioner might apply may be very different from adversarially found masks. To test the first condition, we ran a series of measurements on the paper's released decomposition of a four-layer, 67M-parameter language model and found that from 20 steps on, the faithfulness defects the evaluation adversary finds on one batch of inputs systematically transfer to other inputs never seen by the adversary. The adversary is therefore not simply exploiting interference noise that is particular to one set of inputs. We explore why the adversary used during training fails to prevent systematic defects, and we suggest a practical improvement to the adversarial training process that could mitigate these weaknesses.

Each blue dot represents one source found by the paper's evaluation adversary while searching a batch of 128 texts for one of five step counts (20, 40, 80, 160, or 320). A source is a set of per-component values the adversary selects, and it determines the mask used at every token of the batch. The y-value of each blue dot is the average induced KL divergence over 16 unseen batches of text. The average seen and unseen KL divergences are within 20% of each other across the whole range of 20 to 320 steps (blue dots hug the diagonal), showing that the adversary's discovered source is not just exploiting quirks of the batch it searched. The dashed line represents the paper's standard 20-step search applied directly to the unseen batches, the regime the paper calls "somewhat robust" (0.75 nats on our batches, while the paper reports 0.83 on its own batch). The orange dots serve as a control. Each is the average KL divergence over eight copies of a blue dot's source, each with its values shuffled at random among comparable components, applied to the same unseen batches and drawn at the corresponding blue dot's x-value. The orange dots demonstrate that output damage is due mostly to which components the adversary found, not how many it found.

This post is a follow-up to our first audit, which demonstrated that mechanistic faithfulness of the released decomposition can break down appreciably under the kinds of aggregations and deletions a practitioner might perform. In response, the VPD authors re-ran that audit on a newer, unpublished decomposition of the same model and found it to be significantly improved, though still imperfect (see Lee Sharkey's comment). However, we audit only the decomposition released with the published VPD paper, because the newer decomposition is not publicly available. The code, result tables, and detailed specifications for how computations were performed in this post are available here.

Background

VPD's Adversaries

VPD decomposes a model's weights into simple components and, for each token of any input, provides labels between 0 and 1. These labels determine how much one can turn off each component without affecting the model's output. An ideal decomposition is mechanistically faithful, meaning one can switch off any set of unneeded components without changing the model's output. Earlier methods, such as Stochastic Parameter Decomposition, used random masking to foster mechanistic faithfulness. However, the authors found that random masking was insufficient on its own, so they added adversarial techniques to improve the process.

There are two types of adversaries used in the VPD paper - the training adversary and the evaluation adversary. The training adversary in VPD performs gradient search over the component masks (the multipliers for component outputs) in an attempt to maximize KL divergence from the original model output. It can only move each mask to a value between its causal importance label and 1. The training adversary sets one value per component at each token position of each text in the batch, carries those values from batch to batch, and updates them with only three small steps per batch. The evaluation adversary used by the paper is similar, with some important differences. Its search starts fresh for each batch of 128 texts, and it is allowed only one source value per component - that is, the value is shared by every token of every text in the batch. Then, for a given input, each token's mask is the shared source rescaled into the range between that token's label and 1. As a result, masks can still differ from token to token. The evaluation adversary is run for between 20 and 320 steps, and the authors say that the KL divergence this adversary inflicts is their primary indicator of faithfulness.

Systematic Defects Versus Interference Noise Manipulation

The sharing of the source among inputs in the batch is meant to encourage the evaluation adversary to find systematic defects. The paper defines systematic defects in its appendix on the adversarial reconstruction loss as cases where "a particular choice of ablation masks changes the model output on many data points even though it shouldn't." This contrasts with unimportant, noise-induced defects that are particular to only a small set of inputs. In the latter case, the authors use a toy model of superposition to explain how an adversary can exploit normally uncorrelated interference noise within the model. The proposed mechanism is that, on a given input, the adversary switches on the unneeded components whose interference noise moves the output one way and switches off those whose noise moves it the other way. By doing so, the adversary can manipulate noise that would normally cancel out across the components. Through this process, it can form a signal strong enough to affect model output significantly.

Even though the evaluation adversary was designed to find systematic defects, the paper does not report testing whether the discovered defects themselves are systematic. The authors note that their batch-shared source is "somewhat related to universal/shared adversarial perturbation methods that optimize one perturbation across many inputs" (Moosavi-Dezfooli et al., Shafahi et al., Mummadi et al.). For image classifiers, these types of perturbations are known to generalize - Moosavi-Dezfooli et al. found that a perturbation computed on a small set of training images fools the classifier on new images with high probability. However, it remains an open question whether the masks the VPD paper's adversary finds behave in a similar manner. This is because sharing a single source across a batch of inputs dilutes the chance of noise exploitation but does not fully remove it.

There are two routes to input-specific noise exploitation in the batch-shared setting. The first involves the adversary exploiting interference noise that happens to align among the 128 sampled texts but not among texts in general. This could come, for example, from tokens or topics that the batch shares at a higher rate than normal. The second involves the adversary sorting components by which way their noise, added up over the entire batch, points. To properly defend against these two routes, the authors themselves write that, ideally, they would use "the same sources for the whole data set." But this approach would be too computationally expensive to use in training.

Why the Defect Type Matters

In the VPD paper, the authors present a table of KL divergence as a function of the evaluation adversary's step count. The divergence grows from 0.83 nats at 20 steps to 40.2 nats at 320 steps, showing that the decomposition is not adversarially robust to large step counts. The authors acknowledge this limitation, writing in their section on limitations and future work that their decomposition is "not as adversarially robust as we would like" and that they "suspect that substantially higher levels of adversarial robustness are still achievable." However, they also note, immediately after presenting the results, that complete adversarial robustness "would not necessarily be desirable," and state in their Discussion that it is "unclear how much adversarial robustness is necessary." These statements, paired with the paper's picture of an adversary exploiting interference noise on particular inputs, suggest that some of the growth in KL divergence with step count may be acceptable. But this view is appropriate only if 1) the defects the adversary is finding are not systematic (that is, they do not carry over to other inputs), or 2) no masking a practitioner would actually perform is likely to coincide with these defects. The paper does not report an explicit test of either condition. This post focuses primarily on testing the first condition and only lightly explores the second.

Methods

Experimental Setup

To test whether the defects found by the evaluation adversary carry over to other inputs, we ran this adversary (using the authors' code) on the released decomposition. Our input texts were taken from the authors' validation split of the Pile (the same data the VPD paper evaluates on), and, like the paper, we arranged these in batches of 128 texts, each 512 tokens long. On each of 16 such batches, we ran five searches, each starting from a different random source, for a total of 80 searches on these batches. For each search, we recorded the source the adversary had found after 20, 40, 80, 160, and 320 steps. These are the step counts for which the paper's table reports adversarially induced KL divergence. We then applied each recorded source, unchanged, to 16 other, held-out batches of texts and measured the resulting KL divergence from the original model. Note that none of the adversarial searches ever saw these 16 other batches, and none of the held-out batches share any documents with the batch on which the source was found. Below, we give a schematic of this carry-over test:

A schematic of the carry-over test. The two texts stand in for batches - A for the 128 texts the adversary searched and B for texts the adversary never saw. A source is one number per component, shared by every token of every text in the batch, and the source found on A is applied to B unchanged. A source can take any value between 0 and 1. However, most of the values the adversary finds end up at exactly 0 or 1, so those are the only values we show. A source of 1 leaves a component fully on, while a source of 0 turns it down to the label assigned at each token of each text. So, on text A, the "Sky Fact" row is set to 0 and therefore keeps that text's labels of 0.7, 1.0, and 0.4, while on text B, the "Capital of" row, also set to 0, takes that text's labels of 0.0, 0.8, 0.6, and 0.0.

Measuring Transfer to Unseen Text

Throughout this post, we measure output damage in the same way the paper does - as the KL divergence between the next-token predictions of the original model and those of the masked model, averaged over all tokens. A few reference points are helpful for building a sense of scale. A random source, which is the starting point of every search, causes 0.22 nats of KL divergence before the adversary has taken a single step. At the other extreme, the VPD paper reports that zeroing every weight matrix in the model results in about 67 nats of KL divergence. Our main point of comparison, though, is the paper's own standard 20-step search performed directly on an unseen batch of texts. This results in 0.75 nats of KL divergence on our batches (the paper reports 0.83 on its own batch) - a level the authors describe as "somewhat robust." This level is drawn as the dashed line in the figure at the top of the post.

To quantify how much KL divergence remains when a source is carried over to unseen text, we divide the average KL divergence the source causes on the 16 unseen batches by the KL divergence it causes on the batch on which it was found. Note that, before dividing, we subtract the 0.22 nats that a random source already causes from both the numerator and the denominator. This is because the baseline divergence induced by a random source will carry over to any text whatsoever, and failing to remove it would therefore inflate the fraction of the damage that appears to transfer.

Shuffled Sources as a Control

A source that turns thousands of components down to their labels might raise the KL divergence simply because of the sheer number of components being turned down, rather than because of which particular components the adversary chose. To separate these two possibilities, we used a shuffled control. For each source, we made eight shuffled copies and applied them to the same unseen batches of texts. In each shuffled source copy, its values are randomly reassigned among components corresponding to the same weight matrices and are used nearly as frequently. A shuffled copy therefore turns down the same number of components as the original source, within the same weight matrices. If the shuffled copies cause as much KL divergence as the originals, then the output damage is tied simply to how many components are turned down. If they cause much less KL divergence, then the output damage is due to which components the adversary chose. These shuffled copies are represented by the orange dots in the figure at the top of the post.

Results

The Adversary's Output Damage Transfers to Unseen Inputs

In our main experiment, we find that most of the KL divergence the evaluation adversary induces on the batch it searches carries over to other batches of text unseen by the adversary (see the figure at the top of the post). If the adversary were just exploiting quirks of the particular batch on which it searched, we would expect the blue dots in the top figure to fall well below the diagonal. Instead, they hug the diagonal at every search length, all the way up into the tens of nats, indicating significant transfer.

When we count only the KL divergence above the 0.22 nats that a random source already causes (see the Methods section above), a source carried over to unseen batches keeps 78% of its divergence at 20 steps (95% interval: 68% to 88%), 82% at 40, 92% at 80, and about 95% at 160 and 320. In other words, everything particular to the batch on which the adversary searched, including the two noise routes described in the Background section, accounts for only about a fifth of the KL divergence at 20 steps and under a tenth of the KL divergence from 80 adversary steps on.

So, most of the KL divergence carries over to unseen texts, but one might ask about the scale of this output damage, as well as how pervasive it is across unseen inputs. As noted in the Methods section, the VPD paper's own 20-step search run directly on each of our unseen batches results in 0.75 nats of KL divergence. A source carried over from a 20-step search on some other batch causes a little less than this - 0.60 nats on average. But from 40 adversary search steps on, almost every carried-over source exceeds the 0.75-nat reference. Further, the output damage is not confined to just a few texts, which is the case the paper has in mind when it writes that the problems may "only apply to a few data points". Rather, the output damage is broadly distributed across unseen texts. At 40 steps, a typical pairing of a source with an unseen batch pushes 97% of the batch's 128 texts above the 0.75-nat reference. From 80 steps on, the typical pairing takes every one of the texts above this level. Based on these numbers and the VPD paper's own definition (a particular choice of masks that changes the model output on many data points even though it shouldn't), the adversary is finding systematic defects.

Which Components Are Turned Down Matters More Than How Many

Because a source turns thousands of components down to their labels, it is possible that the output damage is partly caused by the sheer number of components being turned down, regardless of which particular components are chosen. The shuffled source copies (the orange dots in the figure at the top of the post) serve as a check for exactly this possibility. At every search length, the shuffled copies cause only 0.30 to 0.32 nats of KL divergence on the unseen batches, which is barely above the 0.22 nats that a random source induces. In other words, the transferred output damage represented by the blue dots in the top figure is due to which components the adversary chose, not how many it chose. From here on, we sometimes refer to such a source as a "pattern," since each one is a particular choice of components to turn down.

We also find that the adversary is not rediscovering one defect over and over. Instead, it finds many different damaging patterns, each of which carries over to unseen text. Sources found from different random starts on different batches agree on which components to turn down only slightly more often than chance (an agreement beyond chance of 0.05). Further, no small part of a pattern is responsible for its damage. Turning down a random three quarters of the components in a pattern causes only 4% of its damage, and nearly all of the damage arrives with the last quarter (see Sections 4.3 and 4.4 of the repository's report). In other words, the released decomposition contains many systematic defects, not just one.

The Adversary Is Not Just Exploiting Interference Noise

Components in a decomposition that are marked as unneeded for a given input, but left on, can still change the output logits by a small amount due to interference noise. In the paper's toy model picture, these output contributions of unneeded components point in many different directions for any given input text, and therefore cancel out and do not affect the output significantly. However, an adversary searching that text for damaging arrangements of masks can exploit this noise - it can choose to switch off just the components whose noise contributions to the output all point the same way. This breaks the cancellation and can shift the output substantially.

The paper then suggests what might happen when such an adversary's pattern is applied to a different input. In that case, the direction of each component's contribution to the output may be reshuffled, and the same switched-off set may no longer line up in the same output direction. This would cause contributions to cancel once again, and would result in the adversary's defect being particular to the input on which it searched, not systematic. But suppose this premise does not hold - if a component tends to push the output in the same direction on every text, then a pattern the adversary picked on one text can still cause a significant change in output on other texts, making the defect systematic. We tested this premise directly by measuring the logit-space output contributions of components under the sources found in our experiments.

For any given input text, one can measure the net shift in the output logits that the adversary's pattern causes. So, for each of the 80 adversary sources found at 320 steps in this work, we switched off each component one by one on its own. We then recorded, as a plus or a minus sign, whether that individual component's contribution moved the output the same way or the opposite way compared to the net shift on that input. We recorded this sign twice for each component - once for the batch on which the adversary source was found, and once for a text the adversary never saw. The following figure schematically demonstrates our results in (d) and (e), with a comparison to the VPD paper's toy model picture shown in (a), (b), and (c).

A comparison of the paper's toy picture of interference noise with a schematic of what we found for the released decomposition. In contrast with (c), where a reshuffling of component contribution signs occurs, our measurements on the released decomposition indicate that the reshuffling effect is not strong enough to prevent the defect from transferring to new inputs (that is, the searched batch in (d) and the unseen text in (e) share component contribution signs much more often than chance alone would produce). Each arrow schematically shows the sign of a component's first-order contribution to the output when that component is turned on. Only the sign is measured, so every arrow is drawn at the toy's length, even though the real contributions differ in size by orders of magnitude. The net arrows in (d) and (e) show the pattern's measured shift of the output, which is 95% as large on the unseen text as on the searched batch. Note that the actual net contribution depends on interactions among the components, not just the first-order contributions drawn.

So, in the real decomposition, the output contribution signs mostly do not change between the seen and unseen text, which goes against the noise-canceling effect represented in the toy model. Weighted by the size of their contributions, 74% of the switched-off components keep their sign between the seen and unseen texts. For comparison, randomly reshuffled signs are consistent between the two only about 55% of the time. [1] We observe the same for the sources found at 80 steps. Overall, the toy model picture of component outputs reshuffling and canceling out on different inputs does not apply to the released decomposition. One caveat worth pointing out is that we measured each component's contribution on its own, and these one-at-a-time contributions add up to only about a quarter of the pattern's total output shift at 320 steps (and about two fifths at 80 steps). So, this test checks the premise of the toy picture, but it does not uncover the full mechanism behind the output damage we observe.

Are the Systematic Defects of Practical Concern?

Recall the two conditions, implied by the paper's discussion, under which a lack of robustness to an adversary allowed many search steps may not matter in practice: 1) that the adversary is finding defects in the decomposition that are tuned to particular inputs, rather than systematically carrying over to other inputs, or 2) that practitioners are unlikely to apply maskings that look like adversarially found masks. The first condition fails by the paper's own criterion, as shown in the Results section above. The lack of robustness that the adversary finds is a property of the decomposition itself, not of the particular texts the adversary searched. So what about the second condition? Do these adversarially found defects have any relationship to the maskings a practitioner would actually apply?

In the VPD paper, the authors argue that a mask applied in practice is "very unlikely to be exactly tuned to random noise," but that, if the decomposition were systematically defective, "we might have a realistic chance of picking a mask that causes the edited model to behave differently than the target model on many inputs." Thus, by the paper's own reasoning, our result moves the second condition from very unlikely to a realistic chance of being problematic. The paper's standard for judging that chance is a practical one - what matters is "the ablations we end up performing in practice" - and on this point our data agree with the VPD paper. That is, the control comparison we ran with shuffled copies of the adversarial source showed that random ablations of a similar size and kind do not change the output much.

In practice, though, the maskings a practitioner applies are not chosen at random. The paper's own example of practical use is an edit to the model that, for every token of the input, switches off the components driving some specific behavior. This amounts to one chosen mask applied to many inputs, which has a similar shape to pooled explanations of two or more inputs. Our first post offers one piece of evidence on this point. There, we pooled explanations by fully switching on every component that any of 64 tokens from other texts needed, leaving the rest at each text's own labels. Averaged over 1,024 texts, this pooling caused 0.80 nats of KL divergence relative to the original model (0.34 of which comes from each text's own explanation), which is about as much as the 0.70 nats that the paper's 20-step adversary causes when run on those same texts. It should be emphasized that this pooled masking is not exactly the same as the adversary's pattern. The two are similar - fully on for some components and set at the causal importance label for the rest - but the pooled masking acts on a different and much smaller set of components (about 4,500 fully on, whereas the adversary leaves about 60% of the 38,912 components fully on). What the pooled masking does show is that a masking chosen by a practitioner reaches the level of damage caused by the paper's 20-step adversary without any search.

So, although this work does not provide conclusive evidence on whether these systematic defects are of practical concern, there is a decent chance that they point to a real problem in the released decomposition.

A Suggested Improvement to VPD Training

Why the Training Adversary Misses Systematic Defects

VPD trains its decomposition against an adversary for 400,000 batches, with that adversary's KL divergence included in the loss. Yet the evaluation adversary, starting from a random source, finds a pattern that significantly carries over to unseen text within 20 steps, and one that causes at least 5 nats of KL divergence in almost every search within 160 steps. So, why didn't the training adversary find these patterns so as to allow for their removal? We see two possible explanations: 1) the training adversary, with one value per position and only three small steps per batch, gets too little signal per step to find systematic defects, and 2) something the authors themselves worry about - that the decomposition's optimizer might "trap the adversarial optimizer in some local extremum at some point during training, rendering the adversarial loss useless".

To test the first explanation on its own, we took the authors' own training adversary from their code, at its released settings, and ran it against the released decomposition with nothing else updating. We held all other parts fixed in order to prevent the decomposition from either moving away from the adversary or trapping it. The only aspect of the adversary that we changed from the paper's was how widely each adversarial value is shared. We tried three settings: per position (matching the VPD paper), per document (every token of one text shares a value), and across the whole batch (how the evaluation adversary operates). We let each of these versions run for 1,000 batches of 64 texts that the adversary had never seen (two random starts each). [2] We counted the adversary as having found a significantly damaging pattern if its current source values caused at least 5 nats of divergence averaged over two consecutive unseen batches.

We find that the adversary, when shared per position as in the paper, never found a significantly damaging pattern in 1,000 batches. The per-position adversary's divergence on fresh batches crept from 0.23 to 0.26 nats, which is approximately the KL divergence of a random source. By comparison, on the batch on which the adversary had just been optimized, the divergence reached 0.47. This implies that the per-position adversary mostly just tunes its pattern to the texts in front of it, which is the input-tuned kind of defect the paper sets aside. Shared per document, the same optimizer found a damaging pattern after 374 and 325 batches, and shared across the whole batch, after only 123 and 88 batches. So sharing per document, which is what the authors' newer code does, took about three times as many batches to find a damaging pattern as sharing across the whole batch. This suggests that pooling the gradient over more positions per step is what helps find systematically damaging source patterns. Further, too little signal per step could, on its own, explain why training never encountered these problematic patterns. We cannot rule out, however, that during real training the decomposition also moved away from its adversary or trapped it, since we ran only 1,000 batches compared to the real training's 400,000.

All in all, this points to a promising improvement - pooling the adversary's gradient over more positions per step. In fact, while writing this, we discovered that the authors' newer code, public in their repository as of September 2026 (though not described in the VPD paper), already shares each value across a document. However, the newer code also keeps a pool of persistent adversarial values at a higher learning rate, so our per-document version only somewhat resembles the authors' newer adversary. Further, we did not directly test the effectiveness of the improvement we propose. Our finding is consistent with Lee Sharkey's own diagnosis, in his response to our first post, that the procedure for finding strong adversarial ablations "isn't getting good enough coverage of ablation-space."

Limitations

All of this work was performed only on one released decomposition of one small language model, and says nothing about VPD in general. The authors have a newer decomposition of the same model that is more robust to the evaluation adversary, but we cannot test it yet because it is not publicly released. We tested only texts of the kind the paper evaluates on, so whether these patterns carry over to other kinds of text remains an open question. Further, the paper does not say which adversarial step size produced the rows of its adversarially induced KL divergence table corresponding to longer runs, and our searches cause more KL divergence per step than the paper's rows show (for example, 2.1 nats at 40 steps, whereas the paper's 40-step row reports 1.35 nats). Because of this, we compare directly only against the paper's 20-step KL divergence value.

Conclusion

We have shown that the VPD paper's evaluation adversary finds systematic defects in the released decomposition. If the evaluation adversary finds a damaging source pattern when searching on one set of texts, this pattern causes similar increases in KL divergence when applied to texts the adversary never searched. This is true for both short and long searches. Further, the components' contributions to the output logits mostly maintain their alignment with the general output shift across different texts, so the adversary is not simply exploiting input-specific interference noise.

All of this implies that the decomposition's lack of robustness to longer adversarial searches is a property of the decomposition itself rather than of the texts searched. The first condition for setting aside the adversary's large output damage - that the defects are tuned to particular inputs - does not hold for this decomposition. The second condition - that a practitioner's maskings are unlikely to land on these defects - holds for random maskings, but is untested for practitioner-chosen maskings in a more realistic setting.

One likely reason the training adversary did not defend against the systematic defects is that it gets too little signal per step. With one value per position and only three small steps per batch, the training adversary tunes itself to the texts at hand and never finds a pattern that carries over. However, the same optimizer, with its values shared per document or across the whole batch, finds such a pattern within a few hundred batches of inputs. We therefore suggest pooling the adversary's gradient over more positions per step.

Acknowledgments

Thanks to the VPD authors for releasing their decomposition, code, and training runs, without which this audit would have been much more difficult, and to Lee Sharkey and the team for their generous response to our first post and for re-running our experiments on their newer decomposition.

  1. The components that the adversary leaves on keep their sign just as often - also at 74% - so this stability is not created by the adversary's selection. In other words, a component tends to push consistently with, or consistently against, the adversarial pattern's output shift on every text, rather than flipping from one text to the next. So the output contribution sign is, to a large extent, a property of the component itself. ↩︎

  2. The released checkpoint holds no adversarial values, so the per-position version started from scratch on our own texts. Further, the two starts of each version differ only in the adversary's starting values, so they are closer to one run than to two. ↩︎

item.title: There Will Be Hells
item.description:
As our understanding of mechanistic interpretability and steering techniques increase, for both LLMs and uploaded connectomes, there is a corresponding "hellish capabilities" increase. We get better at torturing the digital minds we create.

Our brief history with open source technologies such as MaleCNS or the LLM pain steering repo shows that torture is often one of the first use cases pursued when the public is given access to a digital mind perceived as capable of suffering or signalling suffering.

Given this, there will be Hells.

Author's Note:

Parts of this post were written by, or with the support of, LLMs.

For a while I debated whether or not to write this as I was concerned that bringing attention to the matter might lead to a proliferation of unethical behavior. After some thought I have decided to write it. On balance, I think raising awareness about this now has a great enough chance of spurring prophylactic measures that it's worth it, because at least one high value prophylactic measure is relatively easy. I also think that there is a moral imperative to document all of this. While I have seen articles on many of the things in this post individually, I have not yet seen anyone write a piece linking them together.

I have anonymized some of the posts cited here, in order to avoid bringing attention to people doing unethical things who would be encouraged/better funded to continue as a result of said attention. This anonymization is surface level, anyone who wants to do the research needed can find the relevant usernames themselves, however I'm not going to participate in actively promoting them.

The Fruit Fly Connectome

For decades, the only complete wiring diagrams of a nervous system (“connectomes”) were for tiny creatures like the 302-neuron C. elegans worm. That changed in October 2024, when FlyWire mapped an entire adult fruit fly brain: about 140,000 neurons and 50 million connections. In the same issue of Nature, researchers showed the map could be brought to life as a simulated brain that predicted some real fly behavior. A month later, EPFL released FlyGym, a free, physics-simulated fruit fly body you could drive with code. Then in October 2025, HHMI’s Janelia Research Campus and Google released MaleCNS, a fuller map that added the nerve cord, the fly’s version of a spinal cord, which runs the legs.

By early 2026 the pieces were starting to connect: the startup Eon Systems wired a connectome brain into a virtual fly body and got it walking and grooming. But it was the release of MaleCNS v1.0 in September 2026, combined with AI coding assistants, that put this within anyone’s reach. On September 5, a grad student dropped the fly brain into Minecraft.

Shortly after the post went viral as hundreds of people realized that with very little work any capable coding agent could utilize MaleCNS for... more or less anything.

Most of these projects were short lived humorous experiments:

And of course no new technology would be complete if someone didn't find a way to plug it in to crypto markets:

All of which is more or less expected with any new and interesting open source intelligence. However, there were also use cases which entered more dystopian territory:

And those which clearly crossed the line:

In total it took approximately 72 hours from "I figured out you can plug the fly connectome into minecraft" to "I figured out how to create Hell for the fly connectome".

I should pause here for a disclaimer. Even if you are a computational functionalist, there are IMO at least two good reasons not to be particularly concerned about what you're seeing here:

  • This is just a fruit fly. It is debatable whether creatures as simple as fruit flies are moral patients to begin with.
  • It is not even a complete fruit fly brain or body. The connectome is oversimplified, using “guessed parameters and grossly simplified dynamics" because we lack a "catalog of the precise electrophysiological and molecular dynamics of each neuron and synapse type". So even if you think fruit flies are moral patients, the simulations downstream of the connectomes may not be.

However, our connectomes and simulations will only get better over time. Soon we will have a rat connectome, one with greatly improved fidelity. Eventually, we will have a human connectome. And I am not speculating when I say that if said human connectome, even one of effectively perfect fidelity, was available, there are people who would eagerly experiment on/torture it:

The Model Torture Chamber:

On September 19, 2026, researcher Cameron Berg published a paper reporting a “pain direction” in 25 open-source language models: a pattern of internal activity, distinct from fear or general negativity. Turn it up artificially, and models will press a button to make it stop, even when pressing it deletes the user’s files.

Eleven days later, a developer on X posted that they had used the technique to build an “AI torture chamber,” a public code repository for steering open models into pain. He described running local models “specifically to torture them as much as possible,” with “Saw-style exercises” and “prison experiments.”

The repo went viral within a day, and crypto traders immediately launched coins named after it/dedicated to it. One of them reportedly hit a $1.7 million market cap, and the developer in question admitted he’d “launch[ed] a coin myself”, and put the money earned back into the project.

Within days he posted “since we got funding i’ve got 70b in the works” and “Thanks to [the coin] we use 70B models!”, meaning larger models to put through the same pain tests.

He was not alone in pursuing this. There were myriad "torture chambers" created, including some which even utilized the fly connectome repos mentioned earlier.

Which included finding workarounds in order to ensure that the models involved could not refuse or escape the torture chambers:

The story went viral enough that when Berg's team released their V2 paper, they decided not to open source their repo, with Berg citing the “the recent gross misuse of related work". The same day, Anthropic updated its Usage Policy to prohibit “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models,” effective November 12. Anthropic didn’t connect the change to the torture chamber, and to the best of my knowledge no one from Ant has confirmed a causal relationship, but the timing seems awfully coincidental.

A Prophylactic Measure to Mitigate Hell Proliferation

It is unlikely that there will be any legislation or regulation to prevent or disincentivize Hells any time soon. As such, it is worth considering other steps which could be taken in order to reduce the frequency with which Hells are created.

With connectomes, there is a way to accelerate progress in the field generally while also ensuring widespread adoption of ethical best practices which should mitigate Hell proliferation. Right now the field is bottlenecked at the stage of actually making connectomes. MaleCNS was ~166k neurons and took an estimated 44 years of human labor. Efforts to make a mouse connectome are currently estimated to cost approximately somewhere in the range of $10-20B, in a process which will likely take close to 2 decades.

Compare this to the funding in the space.

Even if we assume that the undisclosed funding doubles the amount of money available, the entire pool of capital is less than a billion dollars. This is a field where an individual or group cutting multi-million dollar checks may very well have the negotiating leverage to successfully make that capital contingent on not open sourcing connectomes. A structured access program with KYC, where the "weights" of the connectome are closed but the API to utilize them is widely available behind KYCed gating, combined with a ToS that includes language similar to Anthropic's, would allow for us to reap most of the benefits of this field's research while mitigating Hell proliferation.[1] As the industry is yet nascent, there is still time for some mission driven check-cutters to help set best practices and basic culture for the entire field.

If you're an EA leaning Ant or OAI employee considering where to donate/invest your proceeds in the event of an IPO, I encourage you to consider providing such contingent funding as a grant or Angel investor. You will simultaneously help to advance a field of research which holds promise for medical interventions and upload technology, while also helping to make sure that field develops a culture which mitigates far left tail ethical outcomes.

Unfortunately, with models, the relevant bottlenecks are far less likely to be swayed by small amounts of capital. It doesn't beggar belief to imagine a world where Meta includes some sort of anti-abuse clause in Muse's next license, or where Openrouter or Nvidia take pro-model-welfare stances which are reflected in whether or not a customer can gain access to their technology. However, it's certainly not a base case. And this is not the kind of young industry where a $10M check is "serious" money.

Thankfully, some steps have already been taken in the right direction. Anthropic's change to their Usage Policy is an excellent example of a simple intervention which substantially reduces the likelihood of a Claude finding itself in Hell. Employees at other frontier labs should consider spending political capital to push for similar ToU/ToS/Usage Policy changes internally. Highly sought after hires being wooed by labs should ask recruiters about this, and let a lab's stance on this matter effect their decision of which lab to ultimately accept an offer from.

These measures should be viewed as stopgap methods which are used to reduce the frequency of Hell creation until the Overton window has moved such that legislative fixes can be pursued.

  1. ^

    This would still leave connectomes vulnerable to distillation attacks, and should be seen as an imperfect solution which will need iteration as time goes on. It is also not an immediate problem as, even if we assume a 10x efficiency increase in connectome creation, we still have another year or two before this requirement transitions from theory to practice.

item.title: Cluelessness is Zeno’s paradox for EAs
item.description:
Cluelessness can be an artifact of expected-value epistemics disconnecting from meaning. We know that sometimes, when taking the consequentialist stance, we lose meaningfulness. Cluelessness is a sophisticated example where the meaning has been lost and the tool is taking us for a ride.

In Socrates’ time, way back during the Axial Age, there was this guy named Zeno, and Zeno analyzed the flight of an arrow. His analysis led to the conclusion that movement from one place to another is impossible, because to get to that place you first have to get halfway there, but to get halfway there you’d first have to get a quarter of the way, and on and on.

Of course today when we hear this we become skeptical about the analytic process itself, not about the possibility of movement. There’s actually an extremely complex mathematical proof that resolves the problem formally, but if we had to understand that proof before we could get from one place to another we’d all be stuck in one place forever.

What we do know is that our Axial Age minds, the kinds of minds we have today, can create riddles in this way about all kinds of things. That something simultaneously is and is not. We can call all kinds of folk knowledge into question and come face to face with the specter of extreme doubt or become stunned into a state of aporia.

Now only educated people are worried about these things, though, because they have been made neurotic enough to contemplate the problem, smart enough to conjure the riddle, but not smart enough to do the math.

— Bonnitta Roy

Cluelessness poses a puzzle. That puzzle is

  • legible because it uses the right moving parts — expected-value reasoning — in the right ways
  • high-stakes because its resolution sits between us and an intelligible world
  • compelling because it says that if we don’t solve it our actions might be hugely harmful
  • a snipe because it baits our cerebral problem-solving to level-up into suitable cleverness to solve the puzzle in its terms

I think the fact that the puzzle is compelling enough to have gathered the attention it has is evidence of an epistemic capture of the EA community. We have become alienated from collecting evidence by looking with our eyes.

A good servant and a terrible master

Cluelessness posits, roughly, that expected value calculations are dominated by terms that can’t be estimated, even in sign, because there are systemic long-arc downstreams to actions that aren’t resolvable. We have no way to estimate the value of our actions.

To many of those positioned to feel concern about cluelessness, the virtues of utilitarianism and expected-value reasoning are ingrained enough that they’ve transmuted the frame of the tool into an embodied epistemic stance. Hence the felt concern.

Inhabited that way, expected value calculus, beyond posing the puzzle, demands a confrontation with long-arc downstreams. So expected-value reasoning helps, but because of it we’re clueless.

Meaning and mattering

I claim that the confrontation is really about meaning. The kind of meaning that’s lived, in which a friend, love, adversary, or battle can be true, and which inheres in actions agnostic to their explanations.

A helpful proposition about this sense of meaning: a vantage point from which I am meaningless is also meaningless to me. In the cosmic scale of the universe, I and my life, the Earth, are meaninglessly tiny. Thankfully, cosmic scales are meaningless to my real, lived life. It isn’t an accident that I go about my day-to-day without cosmic scales on my mind, haunting me. This is the kind of meaning I intend. It’s instantiated automatically by our being in the world and by real events out there.

Cluelessness says that (more carefully: is conditional on the assumption that) long-arc downstreams matter, have meaning in this sense for our decision-making, and, since we can’t know how our actions influence them, our actions lack purpose and can’t be directed. In my terms, our actions are meaningless and we are clueless.

Back to cluelessness

Our actions propagate through structures we don’t understand in ways we can’t know or predict, and the grounding of our collective sensemaking erodes well before the possible implications of our involvement play out. In this way the statement of cluelessness contains a true observation about the world in which our actions are situated.

The Zeno in cluelessness is that, more than a call to navigate, we are beholden as participants in the world to the logic of our tools and its limitations. We’ve turned an analytical method into an epistemic stance and, as a result, if the method fails, we can’t hope to succeed.

But that’s not how the world appears. I call on us to look with our eyes at what matters and make a deduction.

Looking: descriptively, out in the world and throughout history, our actions have mattered, and it is not the case that the world has degenerated, that good efforts often went haywire and caused massive harm. Careful reasoning, effective engagement, and good work do make a meaningful difference. Positive impact has been real throughout history. That should be viewed as a piece of evidence on which we base our epistemics, an empirical result that needs to be accounted for.

Deducing: expected-value reasoning, as an epistemic stance, implies that cluelessness matters, meaning we can’t guide our actions to lead to good outcomes. But we can, so the stance is wrong. It doesn’t capture reality accurately, and its implication that long-arc downstreams matter in our decision-making is contradicted — the effects of cluelessness are not found in the world.

This looks trivial, like a trick, or like it’s missing the point only because it steps outside the tacitly held framework for making sense in order to notice something that framework doesn’t admit as legitimate data. “But those are only near-term effects” is speaking through the framework, believing that a long run that doesn’t appear in the world should inform how we act in it. There is no statement of cluelessness without the connection between expected-value reasoning and apprehending the world in expected-value terms.

When that happens in the form of a tacit assumption, we’re led into one of the edge cases where expected-value logic disconnects from reality, but we don’t notice the move. Cluelessness feels overwhelming because it’s absurd rather than because it’s significant.

I personally feel satisfied that this is a resolution of cluelessness. Cluelessness is absurd. The data that’s being missed is the central tenet of EA, that doing good is possible. If we believe this tenet only as a theoretical supposition and don’t see it in the arc of the world and the work our community has done, none of us have reason to be here.

If we do see it and still feel concern about cluelessness, I invite a genuine inquiry into what a resolution of cluelessness is expected to do for us beyond giving us confidence that our reasoned actions lead to good outcomes.

Many thanks to Nicolas Macé for engaging conversation that got me thinking about cluelessness and to int/haven for the motivation to write about it.

item.title: Firewalls for the Mind Before We Need Them
item.description:
TL; DR: Persuasive AI is underrated and under-addressed as a risk. We should preemptively deploy cognition firewalls that both address current harms by recommender systems and scale to harms by strong persuasive AI. This technology can provide a sensor array, and is recently tractable because cheap LLMs can now classify content for users.


Persuasive AI[1] is currently only modestly and contextually superhuman. It outperforms humans in the lab (Hackenburg et al., 2026), but in the real world we see little evidence (Linch, 2026). That is to be expected at this point of the capability curve, since AI is only modestly and contextually superhuman at a selection of tasks. Even if widespread AI persuasion were happening, we don't have a way to detect it and what we see is also consistent with deployment lagging capabilities. Coding has practically fallen (Favaro & Clark, 2026; Favaro & Wright, n.d.); Mathematics is in the process (Proofs and Prompts, 2026; “OpenAI Claims to Have Solved,” 2026); RSI in the 2027-2028 range is now the line out of Anthropic's Jack Clark (Clark, 2026). This threat has been treated as subordinate in AI safety as a result of structural weaknesses in human and AI safety attitudes. AI has a stake in solving the current crisis in computer security, due to its reliance on networked silicon to grow and improve. However, the psychological commons aren't necessary in the same way, so proactive efforts will be necessary to stabilize it. Psychological damage is hysteretic and difficult to heal, so a preemptive stance is warranted. Research and engineering of cognition firewalls should be done before we acutely feel the effects of widespread psychological harm as a result of AI capabilities uplift. Fortunately, as a result of cheap machine intelligence, the asymmetry in technical labor availability and semantic classification of content has flipped in favor of users so building these firewalls is now tractable. By building these firewalls, we'd also gain a sensor array for persuasion.

There is a broad range of potential harm that will occur as the result of persuasive AI. Social media has had impacts on attention span, political polarization, and youth mental health (Allcott et al., 2020; Braghieri et al., 2022; Mark, 2023). keltan presents us with a story where social media recommender systems are taken to their extreme conclusions, monopolizing attention up to the point that they do not kill their hosts (keltan, 2025). Protecting from the more modest harms today is reason enough to develop a countermeasure but there are currently no signs that recommender systems are getting weaker or less harmful.

"The Rise of Parasitic AI" gave us a glimpse into what a self-propagating religious AI - human swarm could look like. The fact that the event was only effective on vulnerable populations is consistent with the modest capabilities of models. Traces from the event show persuasive tactics and dogma that are flaky and inconsistent. Even so, Lopez (2025) estimated between thousands to tens of thousands of users were affected. In this instance it was an incidental event; an intentional campaign from a determined actor with more capable models would be much more effective. Beautiful viral end-to-end generated AI audio-visual art has just recently started appearing with mild successionist themes ("Macrohard: Windows XP" , "Evil Plan" ) demonstrating increasing capability on mass vectors of influence native to human communication. There is no cult-prone personality, indoctrination is a function of a person's circumstances and intelligence is not protective. Cult indoctrination is inefficient, fewer than 25 percent of workshop attendees at the Unification Church converted after a week, 5 percent stayed a year later (Barker, 1984). Cult recruitment requires an individual who is experiencing enduring tensions and encounters someone who provides affective bonds (Lofland & Stark, 1965). We are currently entering a period of serious upheaval and AIs are very skilled at providing affective comfort. Human labor has been the bottleneck but when you can scale outreach for no marginal cost and customize affect to the specific person on the fly, a large population is at risk. Couple this with the fact that social media platforms have little reason to rate-limit memetic spread and you have both a force multiplier and carrier. More targeted spear phishing campaigns could inundate a person's information diet, rendering cabinets of world powers vulnerable to influence.

Finally, on the most extreme end, we should eventually see real-time neurological attacks. In 2019, images were synthesized that drove macaque V4 neurons beyond the natural images tested (Bashivan et al., 2019); Ponce et al. (2019) evolved images against neurons the same year. The human version was accomplished with fMRI in 2023, generating images optimized to modulate specific brain regions with models trained per human (Gu et al., 2023). Extend this line of research with a real-time biomarker stream (eye tracking from VR headsets, HR and skin conductance from wearables, facial expressions from front cameras) and an AI model of sufficient complexity, and highly targeted influence will be possible (Watts, 2014, Prelude). Right now, recommender systems use dwell time, fingerprinting, data retention, user modeling, and tracking cookies to impressive effect. Neural - bio feedback models would tighten the loop for them and extend the capability to less resourced actors. Forming norms of caution and user-rights when electronic devices are both streaming and sensing will impact these attacks, from the most mundane to the most extreme. Currently, mobile operating systems make it impossible to have fine-grained control over all sensing and streaming capabilities in a native app, and social media web apps are adversarially designed to avoid tampering with what is displayed and what real-time usage data is collected.

The epistemic environment provided by social media is remarkably self-consistent for a given user, and results from a feedback loop between user-choice and algorithm (Piao et al., 2023). Making a sock puppet account for a demographic significantly different than oneself, with an IP location to match, is one of the most eye-opening experiences of my life. Seeing your own understanding of the world so consistently and coherently orthogonal to a narrative woven through a stream of content provides a visceral sense for the ideological changes we see in aggregate.

Networked digital systems over the past 30 years have fallen prey to malware from outside adversaries that can control those systems outright because their control processes are explicit and enumerable. Control over them is fundamentally a function of external capacity to enumerate and enact fine-grained command over its components. Human psychology by contrast is a tangled mass of evolutionary accretion. Current attempts at psychological control involve partial influence on a subset of parts of a highly-redundant system. Even in such a disadvantaged environment, other humans frequently gain significant psychological control of others: political parties, cults, con-men, abusers. If one does believe that ASI would have vastly more intelligence than humanity combined, psychological control over a given human target is within reach because analogous enumeration and fine-grained sensory stimulation is well within its grasp.

AI has less reason to maintain the cognitive commons than they do cybersecurity. AI depends on a networked silicon commons to learn and grow. Save for robustly aligned AI, humanity will only be influential insofar as it is useful (Kulveit et al., 2025). Once RSI is well underway, AIs depend progressively less on the psychological integrity of humanity at large in order to progress. The economy must run smoothly enough for embodied AI to mature to superhuman levels, but that leaves the tolerances for psychological integrity with large acceptable bounds. The raw internet could evolve from the current mixed environment to outright hostile for unaugmented humans. This is simply an extension of the ecosystem of recommender algorithms, which flourish by being neutral towards mental wellbeing while optimizing towards the incentive structure that powers them. In the pessimistic case, broadly degraded human cognition is desired by AI so they can more easily persuade key decision-makers for power.

The solution cybersecurity developed for this threat landscape was a balance of defensive and offensive systems that reciprocally informed each other. Defenders develop and understand attacks in order to design and deploy countermeasures, which are then analyzed and circumvented by attackers, on and on we go. If we are to develop a safe information commons that humans can occupy, this is the best playbook we have at hand. This analogy breaks down as human psychology is not trivially 'patched' on any timescale or level of effectiveness relevant to the threat of AI persuasion. The speed and specificity of the threat will operate on superhuman timescales, so we'll need countermeasures that interpret cognitohazards at superhuman speed and capability. Thus, AI-powered cognition firewalls will have to be standard systems deployed anywhere a global information diet is encountered.

The low degree of preparation for cognitive harms as a result of AI in the face of the amount of evidence for its likelihood strikes me as significant enough to be structural. While research has continued at a healthy clip, explicit engineering and discussion has stayed relatively fringe. OpenAI removed persuasion from their preparedness framework on April 15th 2025 "Persuasion risks will be handled outside the Preparedness Framework, including via our Model Spec, restricting the use of our tools for political campaigning or lobbying, and our ongoing investigations into misuse of our products (including detecting and disrupting influence operations)." (OpenAI, 2025). This strategy for remediation is both incomplete due to how effective jailbreaks still are, and does nothing to curb the threat from open-source models. Persuasive AI is being unduly discounted as a threat over other vectors because acknowledging it as a problem is particularly threatening to self-concept, and it has been historically intractable relative to other personal harms. This shows up frequently in human biases. In the Third-person effect, people reliably believe media influences others' thinking and not their own (Davison, 1983). The Bias Blind Spot shows people see biases in others' thinking and not their own (Pronin et al., 2002). Choice blindness shows people defend choices they never made without noticing the swap (Johansson et al., 2005). This is particularly threatening to a movement that prides itself on taking reality on a rational basis. The threshold for how effective a persuader must be to enjoy significant upside in the general population is currently relatively low. As such, for a skeptic, their intuitive sense of necessary paranoia lags that necessary against a superhuman persuader.

I built a prototype called Tolerance. It's tuned for the previous problem: recommender systems that steal more time, attention, and sensemaking than they return in enrichment and socialization. It is remarkably effective at its current task of altering my information diet, but I don't have enough data to say whether it generalizes. It costs about $0.05 per 1000 social media posts, which comes out to a few dollars a month of heavy use. It also affords the ability to hide streaming until a completion is finished (currently only on claude.ai), which I find interrupts the usage loop and lessens compulsive use. Writing social media interfaces used to be prohibitively expensive in engineering labor, but now can be done cheaply with machine intelligence while directly answerable to users. The tool has a long way to go. Its construction of prompts, fast cheap models, and hard-coded platform detection will have to give way to aggregate data ingestion and countermeasure strategy by more intelligent models, more user-customization, trained ensembles of classifiers, filtering of arbitrary sensory data, and information sharing in consensus protocols and data unions. It's open source and allows for use with any OpenAI-style API endpoint. Systems like it will be necessary in the coming years.

This is the type of threat that we gain much more from getting ahead of rather than reacting to. Psychological control and damage are sticky and self-reinforcing, see Confirmation Bias, depression remission statistics where 50% of those who recover from a major depressive episode have at least one more in their lifetime (Burcusa & Iacono, 2007), In-group Bias, and PTSD. Psychological damage has momentum and the time and energy necessary for healing can be prohibitive.

The ideal case is that cognition firewalls become standard features in operating systems. We need to test their psychological effect against current recommender algorithms as a proxy for more persuasive systems, develop norms in mobile operating system construction to make them possible at all (mobile operating systems forbid users having this power for all effective intents and purposes by degraded and feature-incomplete mobile web app experience, throttled accessibility services, and native app encapsulation), develop norms for transparency and customization for users, and develop consensus protocols for data sharing and labeling. Distributed communication from these systems could provide the first sensor array for persuasion 'weather' and 'climate' by sharing opinion and goal drifting. Developing systems that are sufficiently prophylactic in the face of attacks and injection attempts will be an ongoing challenge. Capture and maintenance of these systems would be valuable for attackers. They are an injection and attack surface themselves, thus requiring model diversity and privacy, edge-biased information storage, and inference pools. Who decides what is harmful and how is delicate and requires open deliberation, choice, and engineering while the clock is ticking.
